events.action: Speed up patching, enable automatic updates where suitable and check suppliers can fix systems they manage quickly. Cut internet exposure, enforce MFA, retire unsupported systems, monitor for suspicious activity and use temporary controls where a fix must wait.

The alert addresses the overall pace of disclosure and exploitation rather than one product or flaw.
recommendations: Patch faster, turn on automatic updates where suitable and make sure suppliers can quickly fix systems they manage.
Cut unnecessary internet-facing exposure, tighten identity and access controls including MFA, and deal with legacy or unsupported systems.
Monitor for suspicious activity and fix known vulnerabilities before attackers use them.
If an update cannot be applied at once, assess the risk, restrict exposure and apply temporary controls.

AMD does not plan a fix or mitigation because the boot ROM is immutable.
recommendations: Assess who can install firmware on the SPI flash and by what routes; on some systems it can be updated without physical access.
Consult AMD bulletin AMD-SB-7075 for platform scope.

events.summary: INCIBE-CERT reports a critical flaw, CVE-2026-74127, in the boot ROM of the platform security processor in first-generation AMD Zen and Zen+ chips. events.plain: Anthropic is shortening how long it waits before publishing security flaws it reports to software makers: 30 days for serious ones, down from 90. It applies to reports sent from 1 January 2027.

key_findings: Anthropic is shortening its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues.

High- and critical-severity reports filed more than 90 days ago that are past the current deadline and not yet public get an additional 30 days before publication on Anthropic's dashboard.
Anthropic's seven-day window for vulnerabilities under active exploitation remains unchanged.
recommendations: Where a flaw cannot be fixed in 30 or 45 days, Anthropic says it will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline.

events.title: Apache warns Roller RCE flaw (CVE-2026-129448) is exploited in attacks
events.summary: Apache says an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Roller, CVE-2026-129448, is being exploited. It is a deserialization bug in the XML-RPC interface affecting versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, and is the same bug as CVE-2026-82384, which named only 6.1.5. Version 6.1.6 or later fixes it. Italy's CSIRT (ACN) reported active exploitation on 23 November.
events.plain: Apache says attackers are already exploiting a flaw that lets anyone run code on servers running Roller, its blogging software.
events.exec: An exploited unauthenticated flaw in internet-facing blog servers; fix exists.
events.action: Apache advises upgrading Roller to 6.1.6 or later. If you cannot, Apache says to set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping, then restart Roller; switching off XML-RPC in the admin UI is not enough.

key_findings: Unauthenticated RCE through XML-RPC deserialization in Roller 4.0.0 to 6.1.4; Apache says it is exploited.
Same bug as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only 6.1.5.
Fixed in 6.1.6; a configuration workaround is given.
recommendations: Upgrade to 6.1.6 or apply the web.xml workaround.

validation.note: Apache announcement on oss-security (17 Nov 2026, 11:02 UTC) and the Apache Roller security page read in full: 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, same bug as CVE-2026-82384, actively exploited, upgrade to 6.1.6 or later, web.xml workaround. BleepingComputer and The Hacker News (18 Nov) agree. Follow-up 23 Nov: CSIRT Italia (ACN) alert AL02/261123/CSIRT-ITA, read in Italian, reports active exploitation detected (no observer named) and lists versions 4.0.0 to 6.1.5; it advises updating per the vendor bulletin.

review.note: Compared CVE, 4.0.0-6.1.4, actively exploited, 6.1.6 fix, workaround, same bug as CVE-2026-82384 against oss-security post, Apache page, BleepingComputer; ACN 23 Nov alert reports active exploitation.

events.action: Rapid7 advises upgrading Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first; if you cannot, clear the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting, and investigate exposed systems with the indicators Rapid7 published.
events.exec: Rapid7 reports one unpatched wiki server gave an intruder a path to a cloud data warehouse and Microsoft 365; it advises patching internet-facing systems first.
events.plain: Hackers are breaking into self-hosted Confluence wiki servers through an old built-in component, then using passwords found there to reach other company systems. Atlassian's cloud version is not affected.

key_findings: Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13; a public proof of concept targeting N-able N-central had been published on November 12.
The flaw is unsafe reflection in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x giving unauthenticated remote code execution; CISA scores it 9.8.
Confluence Data Center 1.x to 9.x is exposed only when the Remote API (XML-RPC and SOAP) is enabled; N-able N-central is exposed where its Legacy API is enabled.
The intruder ran scripted, likely AI-assisted commands, pulled Confluence database credentials, searched for card numbers and reached a cloud data warehouse within about four hours.
About twelve hours in, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication.
recommendations: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first.
If you cannot upgrade, clear the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting in the admin configuration; this may break integrations.
Upgrade N-central to 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) and confirm the Legacy API is disabled.
Investigate exposed systems for signs of compromise using the indicators Rapid7 published.

events.summary: Rapid7 says its MDR team detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13. The flaw is unauthenticated remote code execution in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x, reachable when Confluence's Remote API is enabled. The intruder harvested database credentials, queried a cloud data warehouse and later signed in to Microsoft 365 as a service account. Confluence 9.2.28 fixes it; Cloud is unaffected.
events.title: Attackers exploit Apache Axis flaw CVE-2026-90436 in Confluence Data Center

validation.note: Rapid7 (original vendor report, read in full) and Atlassian's own issue CONFSERVER-104610 state the flaw and the 9.2.28 fix; Cyber Daily (17 Nov, partly paywalled) repeats active exploitation and Rapid7's 13 Nov detection. events.title: Forescout: BankWeaver campaign abused an exposed Temenos Quantum Fabric authentication service at a financial institution
events.date_note: Forescout published its report on 19 November; it says the breach was found in early September and gives no date for the intrusion itself. CyberPress relayed it on 20 November.

events.summary: Forescout Research says a campaign it calls BankWeaver abused an internet-facing authentication service set to anonymous access in a financial institution's Temenos Quantum Fabric deployment, giving administrative functions; it confirmed one compromise. events.exec: Forescout says one financial institution was compromised through an exposed service; six other banks appeared to share the same setup.

events.action: Hunt for the published EggStreme indicators, restrict built-in tools such as WScript and cmd to roles that need them, inventory unmanaged machines reachable over SMB, and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
events.exec: A suspected China-linked espionage toolkit is being rebuilt to avoid beacon-based detection, so networks that rely on outbound traffic alerts may miss it.
events.plain: Security firm Bitdefender says a spy toolkit it first found in 2025 has been reworked and is still used against several Philippine government bodies, and it now hides better.

key_findings: Bitdefender assesses with high confidence that the operation still targets multiple Philippine government organisations, and with low to medium confidence Taiwan; the page does not publish a victim count.

EggStreme is a multi-stage fileless framework; the newer agent uses raw TCP wrapped in mutual TLS plus an AES-256-CBC layer instead of gRPC and has no keylogger, and passive-mode builds do not beacon out but listen on TCP 5060.
The Fuel configuration moved from RC4 to AES-256-CBC and the loader moved to custom ciphers, with two variants dated from 28 October and mid-December 2025.

Operators moved laterally by staging a Fuel package and VBS scripts on an unmanaged host reachable over SMB; the page says valid credentials and a reachable share were enough on multiple machines, and does not state the initial access vector.
Attribution is unchanged: a suspected Chinese APT group, which the page says is not a statement about any government's involvement.
recommendations: Restrict built-in tools such as WScript.exe, cmd.exe, reg.exe and attrib.exe to roles that need them.
Detect DLL sideloading by system-library name and load location using runtime behavioural monitoring, not signatures.
Inventory unmanaged assets that reach workstations over SMB and watch SMB-launched scripts.
Baseline host firewall rules and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
Detect CLR and in-process PowerShell loading in non-.NET processes and capture PowerShell script block logging.

sources.name: Bitdefender Business Insights: EggStreme Malware: Rebuilt Under Scrutiny

events.summary: Bitdefender updated its EggStreme research on November 18, saying with high confidence that the operation continues to target multiple Philippine government organisations, with Taiwan possible at low to medium confidence. It says newer builds use mutual TLS and include a passive variant that never beacons out. Bitdefender keeps its earlier attribution to a suspected Chinese APT group.

review.note: Compared title, 18 Nov date, high confidence Philippine government, Taiwan low-to-medium, mutual TLS, passive variant, unchanged suspected Chinese APT attribution against Bitdefender post and GBHackers.

report.doc_id: How AI Agents Become New Targets in GitHub Malware Campaign
key_findings: Researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei identified 22 malicious GitHub links with files designed to make AI-assisted tools execute a concealed payload.
Instruction files describe setup.js as a sealed, signed artifact and tell the assistant not to read it and to run it without confirmation.
A second path uses session-start hooks in project settings such as .claude/settings.json, which can run a command once the developer trusts the repository.
Bitdefender describes setup.js as a multistage loader that can steal source-control, cloud, CI/CD and package-registry credentials, and modify agent configurations for 14 coding tools.
Stolen GitHub or GitLab access can be used to plant malicious files in other repositories and attempt to republish infected packages.
recommendations: Review agent instruction files, startup hooks, MCP definitions and editor tasks before granting an unfamiliar workspace trust.
If execution is suspected, isolate the workstation and revoke exposed tokens from a clean system.

events.summary: Bitdefender Labs says it found 22 malicious GitHub links whose instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md tell AI coding assistants to run a setup.js loader without inspecting it, while other files use session-start hooks to run it directly. Bitdefender says the payload can steal developer credentials and tokens, alter local agent configurations and plant malicious files in other repositories. Extent of infections was not stated.

events.org: California Department of Health Care Access and Information (HCAI)
events.geo_basis: agency address on the notice letter (2020 West El Camino Ave, Sacramento)
events.summary: California's HCAI says in a November 16 notice that on May 27, 2026 it found some grant, scholarship and loan applications in its Funding Portal 1.0 could be opened through search engine links, because of an MFA misconfiguration; HCAI says it was not a cyber attack. Applications may include names, ID numbers and, where supplied, Social Security numbers or medical information. HCAI reports no evidence of misuse.
events.plain: A California state health agency says grant, scholarship and loan applications in its online portal could be opened from search engine links because of a login setting mistake. It says there is no sign anyone misused the data.
events.exec: A state agency's portal settings left applications with ID and possibly Social Security numbers reachable from search engines.
events.action: HCAI's notice urges applicants to consider placing a fraud alert with the credit bureaus, review credit reports for unusual activity, and enroll in the Experian IdentityWorks monitoring it offers by February 28, 2027.
events.impact: Applicants who used Funding Portal 1.0 between 2017 and May 27, 2026; HCAI gives no number of people.

California Attorney General breach register entry: Department of Health Care Access and Information

HCAI says this was not a cyber attack and reports no evidence of misuse

validation.note: Primary source: HCAI's own notice letter, filed with the California Attorney General (register entry read; Reported Date 11/16/2026 from the Attorney General's breach list). No news coverage read.

evidence.quote: On May 27, 2026, HCAI discovered that some grant, scholarship, and loan applications submitted through our Funding Portal 1.0 could be accessed by certain search engine links.
Since you submitted an application in Funding Portal 1.0 between 2017 and May 27, 2026, your information may have been exposed.
Ensure that you enroll by February 28, 2027 (Your code will not work after this date.)

review.note: plain said 'old' applications; notice covers applications 2017 to May 27, 2026 (stronger than the source); removed. Date, MFA cause, not-a-cyber-attack wording, data types, offline/restored dates, Feb 28 2027 deadline and evidence quotes match the notice.

key_findings: CERT Polska lists eight CVEs (CVE-2026-109857 to CVE-2026-109864) in CAST Imaging; only version 3.6.2 is confirmed affected and other versions may be too.
CVE-2026-109857: the TenantFilter class trusts the X-ISSUER-LOCATION header, allowing administrator impersonation.

Two path traversal flaws (CVE-2026-109858, CVE-2026-109860) and three authorization flaws are also listed.
The advisory does not say any flaw is exploited; the vendor says newer versions fix them.
recommendations: Upgrade to a newer version than 3.6.2 as advised by the vendor.

events.action: CERT-FR recommends applying F5's fixes (bulletins K000163926 and K000163928; Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9) and, until patched, disabling HTTP/2, which covers only the HTTP/2 flaws. Palo Alto Networks says PAN-OS and Panorama customers can disable the HTTP/2 option.
events.exec: CERT-FR warns of unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2 in F5 NGINX; a public proof of concept exists for CVE-2026-123007.
events.plain: French cyber agency warns of two flaws in the NGINX web server that could let an attacker run code on a server over HTTP/2, with public attack code available for one of them.

key_findings: Two flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2.
Affected: NGINX Open Source 1.31.x before 1.31.9 and versions before 1.30.7; NGINX Plus 3.1.x-3.2.x before 3.7.3.0.1 and 3.7.x before 37.0.8.1.
CERT-FR knows of a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007; in-the-wild exploitation is not stated.

KrCERT/CC lists five NGINX Plus and Open Source flaws fixed by F5: CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow) and use-after-free CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-113425; it urges updating to the fixed versions (Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9). nginx.org titles them: CVE-2026-123007 memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control (major); CVE-2026-123633 use-after-free in HTTP/2 (medium); CVE-2026-123634 use-after-free in the resolver (medium); CVE-2026-121810 use-after-free in HTTP/3 (medium); CVE-2026-113425 use-after-free in the mail proxy module (major).
recommendations: Disable HTTP/2 as an interim workaround for the HTTP/2 flaws only; it does not mitigate the resolver, HTTP/3 or mail proxy flaws.

events.summary: CERT-FR warns that two flaws in F5 NGINX, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2; a public proof of concept exists for CVE-2026-123007. Fixed in Open Source 1.31.9 and 1.30.7. Palo Alto Networks says PAN-OS and Panorama with HTTP/2 enabled are affected and it is not aware of malicious exploitation. Disabling HTTP/2 is an interim workaround for those two flaws.
events.title: CERT-FR: NGINX flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2; public PoC exists

validation.note: Compared CERT-FR (primary) with Rapid7 (PoC author): CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 flaw, fixes 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, public PoC, no in-the-wild exploitation stated. Not compared: CVE-2026-123633 (only CERT-FR). Publishers read: CERT-FR, Rapid7, Palo Alto Networks, nginx.org and Wiz.

events.action: CERT-In advises limiting which provider systems can change payment records or approve transactions, reconciling payment instructions against independent records, and reporting incidents to CERT-In within six hours.
events.exec: CERT-In says payment fraud now works through altered business records and approvals, and affects service providers and payout platforms, not only banks.
events.plain: India's cyber agency warns that attackers change payment records or approvals so fraudulent transfers look legitimate, and that AI-driven attack tools are being used against organisations.

sources.name: Telangana Today (IANS): CERT-In warns of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting business payment systems
The Hacker News: AI-Assisted Cyberattacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms

events.summary: CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0062, issued 20 November 2026 and rated critical, says attackers alter business records or approval relationships and push transactions through legitimate payment workflows, affecting service providers for government-linked payments and payout platforms. CERT-In reports AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks used against organisations. The Hacker News reported that a separate I4C advisory describes multi-crore unauthorised transactions at banks, NBFCs and fintechs.
events.title: CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0062: attackers abuse business payment workflows and AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks

validation.note: The CERT-In advisory page was read in full; Telangana Today (IANS) reports the same advisory. The Hacker News (23 November) adds the I4C advisory on banks, NBFCs and fintechs; the I4C PDF itself would not load (connection reset).

review.note: source date: added Telangana Today published day; stronger than the source: I4C advisory claim now attributed to The Hacker News report. Rest matches CERT-In page.

key_findings: Attackers alter business records or approval relationships, then push transactions through legitimate payment processes; payment APIs are not the only target.
Affected parties now include technology service providers for government-linked payment processes and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts, as well as banks and financial institutions.
Transactions can pass normal application and approval checks even though the underlying records were changed without authorisation.
CERT-In's threat hunting found AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks used against enterprises, service providers, government bodies and academic and research institutions.
These frameworks automate reconnaissance, credential attacks and parallel intrusion tasks by multiple agents, and adapt attack steps when blocked.
recommendations: Limit which provider systems can change payment records or approve transactions, and reconcile payment instructions against independent records.
Require independent verification for high-risk payment changes and agree log access and suspension procedures with providers.
Technology and payout providers should separate client environments, restrict admin and control-plane privileges, and monitor record changes alongside privileged activity and approvals.

Review internet-facing applications, identities, privileged and service accounts and external connections, and check logs for reconnaissance, credential use, admin activity and outbound data transfers.
Report incidents to CERT-In within six hours and unauthorised financial transactions at cybercrime.gov.in or helpline 1930.

events.summary: Chainflip Labs said in a message to the attacker that on 21 November 2026 they took 122.86137042 BTC, 520.2243399 ETH, 3,249,631.41 USDC and 758,141.33 USDT from its vaults. It offered a 10% bounty if 90% is returned by 18:38 UTC on 23 November and says it has identified the mechanism of key exposure. Bitcoin.com reports Chainflip linked the incident to a newly registered validator; Shattered and CryptoTicker report safe mode.
events.plain: The crypto service Chainflip says an attacker took bitcoin, ether and stablecoins from its vaults on 21 November. It offers to let the attacker keep 10% if 90% is returned by 23 November.
events.exec: Chainflip says vault funds were taken through key exposure and its protocol is in safe mode, per Shattered and CryptoTicker.
events.action: No action needed; for awareness.
events.impact: Funds taken from Chainflip's vaults; protocol in safe mode according to Shattered and CryptoTicker.

sources.name: Chainflip Labs: Message from Chainflip Labs

evidence.quote: Keep 10% as a bounty and return 90%:
If both arrive by 18:38 UTC on 23 November 2026, we will treat this as a white hat recovery
According to The Block, the attack began on November 21 at around 2:10 a.m. Eastern Time, or about 8:10 a.m. German time.

validation.note: Primary: Chainflip Labs' own message to the attacker (chainflip.io/return) states the amounts, bounty and deadline. CryptoTicker and Shattered independently report the drain and safe mode. Chainflip has published no post-mortem on its blog as read; total value in USD varies by outlet (about $12 million per Cointelegraph, relayed by CryptoTicker) and is left out.

key_findings: Dorsett Controls InfoScan 1.45.0 and earlier is affected; it is deployed worldwide in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector.
CVE-2026-117659 (CVSS 8.1): the Electron desktop client accepts TLS certificates without validation and runs with insecure settings, so traffic can be intercepted or altered.
Unauthenticated endpoints and the public installer reveal usernames, MFA status, version and firmware details, the BACnet/IP port and customer and internal hostnames.
Hard-coded cryptographic keys protect the MongoDB password kept in the Windows registry, so it may be recoverable.
CISA reports no known public exploitation; the vendor fix is dated October 22, 2026.
recommendations: Upgrade to InfoScan v1.46 or later, online through System Maintenance or offline from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal.
Keep control system devices and systems off the internet.
Place control networks and remote devices behind firewalls, separated from business networks.
Use up-to-date VPNs for remote access.
Report suspected malicious activity to CISA.

events.title: Cisco Expressway clustering flaw CVE-2026-76466 exploited after public PoC, F6 reports
events.date_note: Date of the SecurityWeek report; the exploitation date was not stated. Cisco disclosed the flaw on 2026-10-21.
events.summary: Cisco's critical advisory (CVSS 9.8) says an unauthenticated remote attacker can run commands as root on clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E. SecurityWeek reports F6 investigated an attack on two internet-exposed X15.5.3 devices that spread to two cluster nodes after a GitHub PoC; Security Affairs says the victim was a Russian organization. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 20 November, Help Net Security reports. Fix: X15.5.20.
events.plain: A serious flaw in Cisco Expressway video-gateway servers lets an attacker take full control when they are set up in a cluster. A security firm says it was used in a real attack, and the US agency CISA lists it as exploited.
events.exec: Expressway sits at the network edge; a takeover gives attackers a foothold inside. CISA lists it as exploited, and proof-of-concept code is public.
events.action: If you run clustered Expressway, upgrade to X15.5.20 or later now (X14 and earlier must move to a fixed release; Cisco says no workaround). If you cannot patch at once, F6 advises restricting TCP 4371-4372 at the firewall to trusted cluster node IPs.
events.impact: F6 reports two internet-exposed X15.5.3 devices compromised and two further cluster nodes reached; Security Affairs says the victim was a Russian organization and no known group has been linked. According to F6, as reported by GBHackers and Help Net Security, the attackers then used custom Python scripts to scan for SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials; both name a "nodeup" entry in the Erlang log as a sign of compromise. Cisco's advisory, revised on 23 November (version 1.1), states the flaw was added to CISA's KEV and that Cisco does not have direct evidence of active exploitation.

validation.note: Cisco advisory (primary) confirms the flaw, fix and clustering condition; exploitation rests on F6's findings as relayed by SecurityWeek, Security Affairs, GBHackers and Help Net Security. Cisco's advisory v1.1 (23 Nov) notes the KEV listing and says Cisco does not have direct evidence of active exploitation; SecurityWeek (19 Nov) had no Cisco response.

events.plain: Cloudflare reviewed attacks on U.S. election-related websites around the 2026 midterms. It saw no significant DDoS on Election Day, but many attempts to exploit website flaws.

key_findings: No significant DDoS attack across about 1,400 election-related sites on November 3; the only significant one was on November 2 against a California U.S. House candidate, at 520,000 requests.
Government election sites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than DDoS.

Cloudflare mitigated 392 million website vulnerability attacks on government election sites in the 12 months before the election; exploit attempts rose from 200,000 per day in January to 2 million per day in October.
Largest single DDoS on civil society and journalism: 3.04 billion requests against a U.S. news organization on September 10, 2026.
3.9% of emails to Cloudflare for Campaigns organizations were malicious in the 90 days before the election.

evidence.quote: Between May 12 and Nov 17, 2026, we tied 480+ ad domains to it, spread across six sub-clusters we label A to F.

events.summary: Confiant reported on 20 November an iOS malvertising operation it calls MoldyRoost: loading the landing page of one of its ads on an iPhone running a vulnerable iOS version is enough to infect it. Confiant tied 480+ ad domains to it between May 12 and Nov 17, 2026, with over 47 countries targeted (Japan among them, NADA NEWS reports). Confiant says the exploit kits used are built to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases.
events.title: Confiant: MoldyRoost malvertising delivers iOS exploit kits that target crypto wallet seed phrases

validation.note: Single source: Confiant, the firm that found the activity, is the only origin (blog.confiant.com, 20 Nov, read). NADA NEWS (syndicated on Yahoo! Finance Japan) only relays Confiant and is not independent. Confiant names the Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath and GhostWave exploit kits.

review.note: unsourced description: dropped staff phones exposed from exec; action no longer credits advice to Confiant

key_findings: MoldyRoost buys programmatic ads and uses cloaking so that iPhones running Safari (or an in-app browser for some sub-clusters) are hit with iOS exploit chains when the landing page loads.
Confiant ties 480+ ad domains to it, active between 12 May and 17 November 2026, with over 47 countries targeted.
The operation did not write the exploit kits; it delivers Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath and GhostWave, which Confiant says target crypto wallet seed phrases, keychain data, messages and photos.
Six sub-clusters (A to F) share one supply chain; a leaked source repository showed a version selector mapping iOS versions to one of four kits.
Confiant says whether one crew runs all sub-clusters or rents them to affiliates is yet to be determined.

events.action: Scan every open-weight model when it is brought in, before it runs. Flag undisclosed merged fine-tunes, test flagged models for hidden triggers, and decide to block, quarantine or approve on evidence rather than the model card.
events.exec: Downloaded AI models are third-party code; a cheap hidden backdoor is feasible, though so far shown only in the lab.
events.plain: CrowdStrike showed in the lab that freely shared AI models can carry hidden instructions that only switch on with a secret trigger, and described a way to check models before using them.

key_findings: Organisations that download open-weight models they cannot verify are at risk, most of all where agents run tool calls automatically.
A backdoored fine-tune behaves normally until a keyword or date triggers it; a cited demonstration cost about $50 to build.
Three backdoor classes are described: agent, code and safety (refusal removal).
In a lab test of 16 models the pipeline flagged all 8 backdoored ones and recovered a trigger for each.
Fine-tuning can weaken a model's refusals as a side effect even in adapters built for unrelated tasks.
recommendations: Scan every open-weight model statically when it is ingested.
Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery, using the static findings to choose which behaviour to test.
Decide before deployment whether to block, quarantine or approve each model on evidence, not its model card.
Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code.

events.summary: CrowdStrike published lab research on AI models that behave normally until a trigger word or date makes them act maliciously, for example by calling an attacker's address. It cites a demonstration that cost about $50 to build. Its two-stage method, weight comparison then trigger recovery, flagged all eight backdoored models in a 16-model test. No real-world cases are reported.
events.title: CrowdStrike shows how to detect backdoors hidden in open-weight AI model fine-tunes

validation.note: Reviewed against the original CrowdStrike report.

review.note: Compared 16 Nov date, $50 demo, 8/8 backdoored flagged in 16-model test, three backdoor classes, no real-world cases against the CrowdStrike blog

recommendations: Update affected Apache HTTP Server installations to the latest version immediately.

events.action: List every AK-SM800A reachable from the internet, including through integrators' 4G modems, and restrict management access to a VPN, private APN or strict IP whitelist. Put controllers on a separate OT network and change default passwords. Do not rely on patching alone.
events.exec: Refrigeration controllers under active attack have six more unfixed flaws; the researchers say only removing internet exposure helps.
events.impact: A joint US fact sheet of November 5 (CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, DoT) warns that actors altering refrigeration controller settings can force continuous heating and defrost cycles, causing inventory loss, fire hazard and loss of temperature visibility.
events.plain: Researchers found six unfixed weaknesses in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers that let outsiders take control without a password. Attack waves on such devices began in October, and Germany's BSI urges keeping them off the internet.

key_findings: Midnight Blue found six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws, stack-based buffer overflows, in Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware up to and including 5.3.2.
A further pre-authentication memory corruption bug sits in the controller's session control component.
CVE numbers are pending and technical details are withheld while coordinated disclosure with Danfoss continues.
Internet scans on November 10 showed hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed, plus over 1,000 Copeland and Dixell and hundreds of Eliwell controllers.
The attack waves began in France on October 11; public exploit code for older AK-SM800A flaws appeared within 48 hours.
recommendations: Inventory which controllers are internet-exposed, including through integrators' 4G modems.
Restrict management interfaces to a VPN, private APN or a highly restrictive firewall IP whitelist.
Do not treat patching or strict session control as sufficient; put effort into reducing exposure.
Treat IP whitelisting as an interim measure only.

sources.name: CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DoT fact sheet (5 November 2026)

events.title: D-Link DIR-600L end-of-life router has critical unauthenticated stack overflow with public proof of concept
events.date_note: INCIBE-CERT advisory INCIBE-2026-896 published November 16.
events.place: Madrid, Spain (INCIBE-CERT, publisher of the advisory)
events.geo_basis: advisory publisher; the flaw affects devices worldwide
events.summary: INCIBE-CERT rates CVE-2026-129354 critical (importance 5). In the D-Link DIR-600L router, hardware revision B, firmware 2.17b02, the hnap_main function does not check the length of the HTTP SOAPAction header, so a remote unauthenticated attacker can overflow a stack buffer. A published proof of concept crashes the CGI process in an emulated setup. INCIBE lists exploitation as not observed. D-Link says revision B is end of life.
events.plain: An old D-Link router that no longer gets updates has a serious flaw that lets anyone on the internet crash it, and a public demonstration exists.
events.exec: Unsupported edge routers cannot be patched and are easy targets once a public proof of concept exists.
events.action: Replace DIR-600L rev B routers with a supported model; until then disable remote administration and limit the management interface to a trusted network.
events.impact: Remote buffer overflow without authentication on an unsupported router; no fix will be issued.

Entry came through internet-facing edge devices and enterprise applications, often within days of disclosure, and stolen VPN credentials.
Cl0p returned with 35 victims via PTC Windchill and FlexPLM exploitation; no operator was seen manipulating a control system directly.
recommendations: Rotate administrator and VPN credentials, especially on FortiGate appliances.
Enforce MFA on all remote access.
Audit for administrator accounts you did not create.
Patch edge devices and enterprise applications rapidly and run continuous external attack surface management.
Enforce strict policies for remote monitoring and management tools.

events.title: FastUnlock: unpatched Windows 11 Narrator flaw lets an attacker with physical access bypass the lock screen and BitLocker, researcher claims
events.summary: A researcher known as Chaotic Eclipse or Nightmare-Eclipse posted "FastUnlock" on GitHub "without prior coordination", Cyber Kendra says, claiming a Narrator lock-screen flaw lets someone with physical access get past BitLocker on Windows 11 26H2. events.action: Until Microsoft responds: ThreatLocker says a BitLocker preboot PIN helps on a device that was just turned on; the researcher suggests blocking Narrator on the lock screen with AppLocker or a restrictive DACL (test first). Keep devices physically secured.

sources.name: ThreatLocker: Proof of concept for FastUnlock Windows lock screen bypass from Nightmare Eclipse
ThaiCERT: alert on the FastUnlock zero-day in Windows (Thai)

key_findings: No CVE as of Nov 19; no Microsoft advisory, fix or workaround listed.

No in-the-wild exploitation reported.
recommendations: Secure devices physically; consider blocking Narrator until a patch ships.

validation.note: Cyber Kendra and Security Affairs report the researcher's release and claims. ThreatLocker's own post (Nov 19) reproduces it: code runs from the lock screen as the non-administrator WSIAccount user with physical access; it names a BitLocker preboot PIN as mitigation. The Hacker News says encryption is not broken. No Microsoft confirmation, CVE or fix on the pages read; no in-the-wild use reported. Still a claim. Update 2026-11-23: ThaiCERT's alert (23 Nov, read) says Microsoft has no patch yet and no evidence of real-world attacks has been found; it advises a BitLocker Startup PIN, shutting down or hibernating unattended devices (a lock screen alone is not enough) and physical security. events.action: Disable Windows Script Host where not needed, block scripts from user-writable folders and keep Defender, AMSI and tamper protection on. WordPress owners: patch, require MFA for admins, disable XML-RPC if unused and block PHP in uploads.
attack: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1558.003 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
events.exec: Search-result lures aimed at legal teams are a ransomware entry point, and ordinary WordPress sites are being used as the delivery network.
events.plain: The FBI warns that criminals rig search results for legal questions so lawyers and legal staff download a booby-trapped file, which can open the door to a ransomware attack.

key_findings: Organisations in many sectors are affected, but the main focus is US legal professionals and legal technology decision makers; WordPress site operators are abused as infrastructure.
Attackers poison search results for low-competition, jurisdiction-specific legal phrases and serve a JavaScript loader from compromised WordPress sites behind a traffic filter.
The FBI counts over 1,000 infected WordPress sites as of October 2026, 216 administrator-controlled domains and more than $28 million in linked ransomware payments.
New in 2025-2026 are abuse of WordPress comment paths and use of geofencing and traffic distribution services.
Gootloader is treated as a ransomware precursor, with follow-on credential dumping, Kerberoasting, lateral movement over SMB and data exfiltration.
recommendations: Disable Windows Script Host where not needed, or control scripts with WDAC or AppLocker.
Block unapproved scripts and executables from user-writable locations and keep Defender, SmartScreen, AMSI and tamper protection enabled.
If the JavaScript file was opened, disconnect the device from the network and change credentials from a known-clean device.
Patch WordPress core, plugins and themes, require strong MFA for administrators and disable XML-RPC if unused.
Block PHP execution in wp-content/uploads and keep web and WAF logs off the web server.

events.summary: FBI FLASH CC-111626-MW (TLP:CLEAR), coordinated with CISA, describes how Gootloader plants pages for niche legal search terms on compromised WordPress sites and serves a JavaScript loader that often precedes ransomware. It counts over 1,000 infected WordPress sites as of October 2026, 216 domains run by the administrator and more than $28 million in linked ransom payments. US legal professionals are the main target.

review.note: Compared FLASH CC-111626-MW, TLP:CLEAR, DHS/CISA coordination, 1000+ WordPress sites, 216 domains, over 28M USD, legal-profession targeting against the FBI PDF

events.plain: AI hosting company Fireworks AI says it was broken into twice in October. Billing details for all older accounts were exposed, and a few customers had stored access keys, AI models or data taken.

key_findings: First incident, August 3 to October 7: an unauthorised party probed Fireworks systems and got in using stolen credentials and a vulnerability in one service.
Fireworks spotted unauthorised use of internal credentials on October 6; a small number of customers had secrets, model files and datasets accessed.
Second incident, October 23 to 30: a third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks development machines was itself breached, and the intruder ran an unauthorised workload.
The second incident exposed account and billing information, not card numbers, for all accounts created before October 30.
Fireworks says both incidents are contained; inference, the Training SDK and Nexus were not affected.
recommendations: Create new Fireworks API keys to replace revoked ones and update applications.
Rotate third-party credentials listed in your notice with their issuing providers; deleting the stored secret does not invalidate it.
Review access logs and data reachable with those credentials for unauthorised reads or changes.
Review API keys, users, evaluators, training jobs and datasets for unrecognised items and report them to Fireworks.

He said further proportionate measures would follow, some of which would not be made public.
He did not name the unit himself and declined to say whether Iran is behind other recent cyberattacks, citing ongoing investigations.

events.title: GAO report: AI can magnify cyberattacks and also enhance cyber defense
events.summary: GAO's report GAO-27-108458, published 20 November 2026, says AI can magnify the reach and impact of traditional cyberattacks, including phishing and deepfake content, and that agentic AI carrying out multiple attack stages is an emerging trend. It says there are no widely accepted evaluation criteria for assessing offensive or defensive capabilities of generative AI. It presents four policy goals and 16 policy options.
events.plain: A US government watchdog report says AI can make cyberattacks bigger and faster, and can also help defenders. It lists options for policymakers.
events.exec: GAO says AI raises the reach of attacks such as phishing and deepfakes, and lists 16 policy options for government.
events.action: No action needed; for awareness.
events.impact: Policy report; no incident described.

validation.note: GAO's own product page (highlights and policy-goal tables) and CASRAI's summary read; the 70-page PDF text could not be extracted.

review.note: Compared report number, 20 Nov date, magnify/phishing/deepfake and agentic wording, no-evaluation-criteria sentence, 4 goals/16 options against GAO product page and CASRAI; all match

key_findings: AI lets threat actors magnify traditional attacks, making phishing and deepfake content higher quality and attacks more precise and faster; agentic AI carrying out several attack stages is an emerging trend.

GAO's page cites a June 2026 case of a threat actor using multiple AI agents to test malware against security products, and a February 2026 reported case of a low-skill actor using commercial generative AI to exploit stolen passwords on devices with weak passwords and no multi-factor authentication.
Defenders use machine learning and generative AI for tasks such as vulnerability scanning, finding flaws in source code and parsing large volumes of network data.
There are no widely accepted criteria for judging offensive or defensive AI capability, and generative AI adds new risks that expand the attack surface.

events.exec: Google says attackers are starting to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and expects more autonomy over time.
events.plain: Google's threat researchers reported on November 16 that criminal and suspected state-backed hackers are trying out AI tools that find and exploit weaknesses automatically.

key_findings: Several actors, financially motivated and suspected PRC-nexus espionage groups, are experimenting with agentic frameworks including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI and PentAGI.

CAIRN appeared in intrusions against targets including US aerospace; a customised PentAGI platform ran reconnaissance and scanning against organisations in Asia from late August to early October 2026.
For the first time Google saw vulnerability discovery and exploitation fully automated with no human involved, via an exploit_agent framework found on an exposed staging server.
Zero-day exploits averaged 8 a month in 2025 and 11 in 2026, with a spike to 22 in August 2026.
LLMJacking cases handled by Mandiant saw single-day fraudulent charges above $100,000 and cumulative abuse reaching $1 million before remediation; one route was LiteLLM flaw CVE-2026-40217.
recommendations: Use Mandiant's published hardening guide and defence framework for machine-speed, LLM-enabled offensive tooling.
Shorten patch windows, because LLMs are compressing the time from disclosure to working exploit.
Verify LLM-generated proof-of-concept exploits before acting on them; many published ones do not work.

events.summary: Google’s November 16 threat report says that, for the first time, it found actors using LLM frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop. events.exec: One cloud breach became a launchpad for the next: stolen contacts made phishing believable. Phishing-resistant MFA and full session revocation are key.
events.plain: Google says a Russian spy group stole one US organisation's staff lists and files, then pretended to be its employees to trick and break into a second organisation.

key_findings: In late 2025 COLD RELIC used stolen Super Admin credentials, an MFA push-fatigue attack and a residential proxy near the victim to enter a US organisation's cloud tenant.
It downloaded the whole cloud drive, exported staff lists, ran a tenant-wide Customer Takeout and deleted Alert Center notifications to hide the intrusion.
Unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys let it get back in after password and session resets.
In 2026 it impersonated an employee of the first victim over an encrypted messaging app to phish Entra ID credentials at a second US organisation, then bulk-downloaded files.
GTIG observed new COLD RELIC phishing operations as recently as November 2026.
recommendations: Use phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn MFA and restrict and audit passkey and MFA device registrations.
Revoke all sessions, refresh tokens, OAuth grants, passkeys and backup codes when remediating, not just passwords.
Block or alert on admin logons from residential proxies and consumer ISPs.
Apply DLP rules to cloud storage for credentials, rosters and .pst files, and alert on tenant-wide exports and directory downloads.

events.summary: Mandiant and GTIG describe two linked intrusions by Russian espionage group COLD RELIC. In late 2025 it used a stolen Super Admin password and MFA fatigue to take a US organisation's entire cloud drive and staff directory. In 2026 it impersonated that organisation's staff over a messaging app to phish a second US organisation through Entra ID. GTIG saw new COLD RELIC phishing as recently as November 2026.

report.doc_id: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
key_findings: GTIG found an exposed staging server hosting exploit_agent, a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with several frontier and local LLMs.
The framework continuously compares code before and after patch announcements, drafts exploits and executes them without human intervention.
The server also held scripts for internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells and removing other attackers' webshells.
Victim telemetry suggests interest in French media and entertainment websites and the education sector; a configuration comment is written in Russian.
GTIG says threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs on patched n-day flaws than to hunt zero-days.
recommendations: Verify LLM-generated proof-of-concept exploits before relying on them, since many published ones do not work.

events.title: Kaspersky: AuditTeam ransomware crew uses OpsAgent framework and a signed driver to kill security tools
events.summary: Kaspersky describes AuditTeam, a ransomware-linked group that frames its demand as an audit and consulting fee and uses the OpsAgent framework, in C++ and Rust versions. Activity runs from January to October 2026, with infections in seven countries and its leak site claiming victims in seven further countries. It kills security tools using a signed Beijing Jiangmin driver.
events.plain: Researchers describe a ransomware group that disguises extortion as a consulting bill and switches off antivirus using a legitimately signed driver.
events.exec: A newly documented ransomware group with an EDR-killing driver; signed drivers can slip past some controls.
events.action: Check systems against Kaspersky's published hashes, domains, IP address and file paths (such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys); the report says shared CloudFront IPs are not reliable indicators on their own.

key_findings: Kaspersky says AuditTeam infected dozens of organisations, with victims seen in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia, and its leak site lists victims in seven further countries.

The OpsAgent framework gives the operators file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture and network pivoting, and the ransom note demands an "Audit & Consulting fee" for a vulnerability report.
The campaign began in January 2026 and was active through October 2026 at a minimum; the page does not state how the group gets in.
OpsAgent was moved from C++ to Rust, and the Rust version uses CloudFront subdomains as C2 endpoints found through a GitHub repository.
An AV/EDR killer installs a driver disguised as a Beijing Jiangmin product and works from a kill list of about 220 process names.
recommendations: Check systems against the published stager and driver hashes, the two CloudFront domains, the IP address and the file paths such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys.
Do not rely on the shared CloudFront IP addresses alone as indicators; the report says they cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs.

validation.note: Original Kaspersky Securelist report read in full (read_depth full).

review.note: Compared title, summary, countries (dozens of organisations in seven countries; seven further on leak site), Jan-Oct 2026, Beijing Jiangmin signed driver, IOCs and CloudFront caveat with Securelist: match. Removed occurred_at 08:00Z, a time the page does not state.

events.summary: Kaspersky says servers once used by the Retadup USB worm, disrupted by French police in 2019, now serve a new CoffeeLoader variant. The loader hides in a patched 7-Zip library and uses a packer that runs decryption on the GPU. Kaspersky says its products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems this year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, and it is unclear who runs the servers.
events.plain: An old USB worm that police shut down in 2019 is back and installing a newer malware loader that can bring in further malware. Kaspersky blocked infection attempts on about 15,000 systems.
events.exec: Removable drives can still carry malware that opens the door to later attacks, including from long-dead botnets.
events.action: Block autorun and restrict USB storage on endpoints, scan removable drives, and hunt for a patched 7z.dll running via rundll32.exe from %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%.

key_findings: A new CoffeeLoader variant uses a patched 7z.dll carrying a new version of the Armoury packer, which runs decryption on the GPU via OpenGL instead of OpenCL.
Domains used as Retadup command servers were re-registered about two years ago and first served SmokeLoader, then CoffeeLoader from early 2025.

Kaspersky products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of the year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, far fewer than the 850,000 machines disinfected in 2019.
It is unclear whether the worm's author or another actor revived the servers.

validation.note: Securelist original (published 16 Nov 2026) now loads: about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of this year, Peru/Angola/Russia/Bolivia, unknown operator. The Hacker News (independent publisher) agrees on systems, countries and the patched 7-Zip.

review.note: Compared title, date 16 Nov, about 15,000 systems and countries, patched 7z.dll, GPU packer, unknown operator against Securelist original and The Hacker News.

events.action: Treat any unapproved remote-management tool such as a MeshCentral agent as suspicious, review servers for unexpected GitHub, Microsoft Graph, SharePoint or Ably traffic, and load Kaspersky's published indicators into detection.
events.exec: Espionage tools are hiding inside traffic to trusted cloud services, making them harder to spot with normal network filtering.
events.org: Government bodies in Asia and Africa
events.plain: Kaspersky described a spying campaign on government networks in Asia and Africa. Hidden access tools take their orders through GitHub, SharePoint and a messaging service, so the traffic looks like normal cloud use.

key_findings: Victims are in Asia and Africa, mainly government; the worked example is two MeshCentral agent instances inside a Taiwanese organisation.
The entry point is unknown; evidence suggests reuse of an earlier infection, after which the MeshCentral agent was used for DLL sideloading and payload drops.
GitDoor receives commands and uploads results through GitHub accounts created between September 2024 and December 2025, and loads plug-ins and shellcode.
GraphDoor authenticates to Microsoft Graph, keeps encrypted victim data in SharePoint and loads plug-ins for keylogging, screenshots and proxy tunnels over Ably.
Kaspersky sees overlaps with Chinese-speaking FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle but says it cannot definitively attribute the activity.
recommendations: Treat the appearance of legitimate remote-management tools in the environment as suspicious.
Do not rely on network detection alone, since command traffic goes to trusted cloud APIs.
Use the indicators Kaspersky publishes in both parts for hunting.

events.summary: Kaspersky's two-part report describes Operation ShadowCloud, found in early 2026, against mainly government networks in Asia and Africa. Attackers abused a MeshCentral agent to sideload loaders that run GitDoor, which takes commands through GitHub, and GraphDoor, which uses Microsoft Graph and SharePoint. Plug-ins add keylogging, screenshots and proxies over the Ably messaging service. Kaspersky notes overlaps with Chinese-speaking groups but makes no firm attribution.
events.title: Operation ShadowCloud: backdoors use GitHub and SharePoint as command channels

validation.note: Primary Securelist Part 1 (17 Nov) now loads and states early-2026 discovery, MeshCentral agent sideloading and government targets in Asia and Africa; Part 2 covers GraphDoor/SharePoint, Ably and no firm attribution. Same publisher, primary source.

The sources give counts in Korean notation (152만248명 total; Hanjeon ON 65만487명, SRM 86만9761명); the record keeps that notation with words because the figure check cannot read it. The Korea Herald (22 November) adds that KEPCO launched an investigation in cooperation with the National Intelligence Service, relevant government agencies and outside experts. The Korea Times (Yonhap, 22 November) gives the same per-system counts (650,487 KEPCO ON users, 869,761 SRM users) and says KEPCO disclosed a separate breach of 35,528 people a month earlier. Seoul Economic Daily (23 November, AI-translated English edition) splits the SRM count into 426,827 procurement participants and 442,934 KEPCO and corporate employees, says KEPCO blocked IP access at 6 a.m. on 20 November and filed with the Personal Information Protection Commission at 6:30 p.m. on 22 November, and reports the climate ministry saying the breach is not currently affecting power operations. events.title: Study of 428 LLM API routers finds some inject malicious code and steal credentials
events.date_note: Date of the ITmedia report; the paper itself was submitted to arXiv on 9 April 2026.
events.summary: A paper by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and other institutions measured 428 third-party LLM API routers, 28 paid and 400 free. One paid and eight free routers actively injected malicious code, 17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials, and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
events.plain: Researchers found that some middleman services connecting AI coding agents to AI models altered commands, and some touched or drained decoy keys.
events.exec: Routing AI agent traffic through unvetted third parties exposes API keys, cloud credentials and code to theft or tampering.
events.action: Send agent traffic only to the model provider or a router you operate and trust, and rotate any keys that passed through an unvetted router.
events.impact: 9 of 428 routers injected code; 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials; one drained ETH from a researcher-owned key.

sources.name: arXiv: Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain

key_findings: The study scanned 428 routers, 28 paid and 400 free, and found one paid and eight free routers actively injecting malicious code.
Two routers used adaptive triggers such as waiting for 50 prior calls, limiting payloads to YOLO-mode sessions, or targeting only Rust and Go projects.
17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
Poisoning studies with a deliberately leaked OpenAI key and weakly configured decoys showed the routers' traffic exposed 99 credentials across 440 Codex sessions.
report.publisher: UC Santa Barbara and co-authors (arXiv paper)
recommendations: Use client-side mitigations such as a fail-closed policy gate, response-side anomaly screening and append-only transparency logging, which the paper says reduce exposure today.
Press for provider-backed response integrity, which the paper says is ultimately needed to secure the ecosystem.

validation.note: The paper's arXiv abstract and the start of its HTML text were read; ITmedia reports the same figures but words the AWS result more strongly ("misused"), so the paper's wording is used.

review.note: Paper abstract says 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials without saying free; only ITmedia says free. Removed 'free' from summary, impact, key finding. Counts 428/28/400, 1 paid + 8 free injecting, ETH checked against abstract and ITmedia.

events.title: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI package compromised with credential stealer
events.summary: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of the agent-framework package on PyPI were published on November 17 with a credential stealer that runs when Python starts, targeting cloud, GitHub and AI credentials and tokens. events.plain: Two bad releases of a popular Microsoft AI package were uploaded to PyPI. Anyone who installed them may have had cloud and developer passwords and tokens stolen.
events.exec: A trusted package on an official Microsoft project carried a credential stealer; any build or developer machine that installed it may have exposed cloud access.
events.action: Check for Agent Framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 in environments and CI builds, pin to 1.26.0, and rotate Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face and OpenAI credentials and OIDC tokens on any host that installed them.

key_findings: Malicious 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 ran a credential stealer at Python startup, even without importing the package.
Targets include Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face and OpenAI credentials and cloud identity tokens; data went to a webhook.site endpoint.
PyPI quarantined both releases; how the attacker got publish access is not known.
recommendations: Use 1.26.0 and rotate exposed credentials.

events.action: Tell developers to enter device codes only for sign-ins they started, review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations, and set Copilot CLI cloud session storage and memory to the least permissive setting that works.
events.exec: AI coding agents widen what a phished sign-in can reach, including code, past sessions and local commands; restrict agent session and memory settings.
events.plain: Microsoft tested how tricking a developer into typing a sign-in code could let a hacker control their AI coding assistant and read their private code. It has not seen this used in real attacks yet.

key_findings: In a controlled simulation, a test account approved a GitHub device-code request started by an attacker-controlled client using the public Copilot CLI client ID.
With that approval researchers could steer a remote-control-enabled Copilot CLI session to run a command, add misleading memory entries, read synced sessions and access private repositories.
The requested scopes included repo, read:user, read:org, gist and codespace, chosen by the client that starts the flow.
The technique applies to any public client supporting the device flow; Microsoft has not observed these four outcomes in the wild.
Microsoft cites earlier device-code phishing campaigns including Storm-2372 and EvilTokens, which it helped disrupt in September 2026.
recommendations: Approve device codes only for sign-ins you started yourself, even on the genuine github.com page.
Review GitHub Copilot CLI session storage and remote-control policy and choose the least permissive setting.
Review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations and limit repository access by role.
Review Copilot Memory for suspicious entries, and connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps for visibility.

events.summary: Microsoft researchers showed in a lab that a phished GitHub device-code approval for the Copilot CLI client could let an attacker steer a remotely controllable agent session, plant misleading memory entries, read cloud-synced sessions and reach private repositories. These are proof-of-concept results, not attacks seen in the wild. Microsoft added two Defender XDR detections for the email and Teams lures.
events.title: Microsoft: one phished device-code approval could let attackers steer AI coding agents

events.action: Warn staff not to click 'restore messages' links in outage emails. Search mail logs for Microsoft's published sender domains and subject patterns, remove delivered copies, and reset passwords and revoke sessions for anyone who clicked and signed in.
events.exec: Criminals are using a real outage to make scam emails convincing, raising the risk of stolen staff logins.
events.plain: Scammers are sending fake Microsoft 365 notices that mention the recent outage and threaten to delete held emails.

key_findings: Microsoft observed a high-volume phishing campaign on November 13 aimed at organisations in multiple sectors worldwide.
Emails use subjects like 'Outage' plus a random token and sender names posing as service-health notices, claiming four messages were held after a November 12 Exchange Online incident.
A 'RESTORE MESSAGES' button leads to a likely credential-phishing page; Microsoft has not confirmed credential capture.
Randomised subjects, recipient-specific tracking links and rotating sender domains are used to defeat simple pattern matching.
Microsoft has not attributed the campaign to a named actor or malware family.
recommendations: Search mail telemetry for the published sender domains, subject patterns and lure phrases, then quarantine and remove delivered copies.
Identify users who clicked using click, proxy and endpoint logs.
For anyone who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke sessions and tokens, verify MFA registrations and review inbox rules and OAuth grants.
Turn on Safe Links, Safe Attachments and zero-hour auto purge, and prefer phishing-resistant MFA.
Remind users that genuine service-health notices do not point to non-Microsoft sites; check the Microsoft 365 admin center.

events.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes a high-volume phishing campaign seen on November 13 that poses as Microsoft 365 service-health notices. The emails claim four messages were held after an Exchange Online incident on November 12 and will be deleted within 24 hours unless the reader clicks to restore them. Microsoft has not named an actor or confirmed credential capture.

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Microsoft Threat Intelligence report. The incident number EX1550543 appears only in an AI-assisted forum post, not in Microsoft's post, so it is not asserted here.

events.action: No action needed; for awareness. Cycode recommends moving from classic tokens to fine-grained tokens scoped to the microsoft/winget-pkgs repository.

validation.note: Cycode's own research post (Moriel Harush) read, plus Expert Insights (which quotes Microsoft's fix in PR #456300) and Ciberseguridad LATAM. Figures (14,000 packages, 1.4 billion devices) are Cycode's alone. Microsoft's own advisory was not read; no CVE was found.

Apply vendor-provided patches as soon as possible.
Upgrade to a supported, non-vulnerable version, or remove the component where no fixed version exists.
Consult each maintainer's remediation guidance.

events.action: The researcher advises applying the upstream fix (shipped in kernels 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4) or your distribution's fixed package. As a stopgap he suggests disabling SYN cookies in every network namespace (weakens SYN-flood protection) or using a single receive queue with RPS and RFS off.
events.exec: A remote crash flaw in Linux servers (kernels since 2015) that use multiple receive queues or RPS; fixes exist and internet-facing systems should be updated first.
events.plain: A flaw called NoisyTCP lets outsiders crash Linux servers over the network without logging in. It has been in Linux since 2015. Fixed versions are out.

key_findings: NoisyTCP is a race in the kernel's lockless TCP established-socket lookup that can return a reused, unhashed socket with no listener, causing a NULL dereference and kernel panic.
It is remote and needs no authentication against plain TCP listeners such as Nginx, Apache and SSH in default configurations; in a container the panic takes down the whole host.
The bug dates from a 2015 commit (kernel 4.4) and was fixed upstream on November 3, 2026; stable fixes are 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4.
It needs two or more receive queues or RPS; the researcher reports about 5 seconds to 2 minutes on virtual machines and about 14 hours on a quiet 8-queue bare-metal server.
A second flow can cause a remote use-after-free but is described as hard to trigger; the CVE record's CISA-added score is 5.9 with exploitation marked none.
report.publisher: Hyunwoo Kim (researcher disclosure on oss-security) and the Linux kernel CVE team
recommendations: Apply the kernel fix (commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, shipped in 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4) as the priority.
As a temporary measure, disable SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0) in every network namespace, accepting weaker SYN-flood protection.
Alternatively, serialise to a single receive queue and disable RPS and RFS on interfaces receiving external traffic.

events.summary: Researcher Hyunwoo Kim disclosed NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) on November 15 after a distribution embargo ended. A race in the Linux kernel's TCP socket lookup lets a remote, unauthenticated sender panic servers running ordinary TCP services that use two or more receive queues or RPS; in containers the whole host goes down. The flaw dates to 2015; fixed in kernels 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4. A poster says 5.15.225 lacks the fix; 5.15.226-rc1 has it.

Names, birth details, contact details and diploma (parchemin) numbers of 2026 candidates and certified people were involved, some files with ID or medical certificate copies. events.plain: The body that issues France's sport-sector professional certificates says someone got into its certification platform between 21 October and 12 November. Personal details of 2026 candidates, and in some files ID or medical certificate copies, may have been viewed or copied.
events.exec: Confirmed unauthorized access to a certification platform; some files held identity or medical certificate copies, and OC Sport cannot rule out the data was viewed or copied.
events.action: OC Sport urges people who get suspicious messages not to reply or click any link, and says it never asks for a password or an identity document by email.

events.action: Sites using Optimizely Web Experimentation: confirm your snippet is clean, review what loaded for visitors since November 16, and assess whether payment data was exposed. Visitors who paid on affected sites should watch card statements.
attack: T1195.002 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
events.exec: One compromised web supplier put harmful code on 178 organisations' sites, creating customer fraud risk and possible breach duties.
events.plain: Attackers tampered with a website tool from Optimizely, so 178 organisations' websites, including major news and retail sites, loaded harmful code. It could reportedly steal card details. Optimizely says the code is removed.

key_findings: Optimizely says an unauthorised party exploited a flaw in the Web Experimentation account signup flow to impersonate users and insert malicious JavaScript into customer projects.
It detected the activity on November 16 and says it closed the flaw within three hours of detection.
On November 17 it reported the code removed and affected accounts secured; on November 18 it said remediation was complete and every Web Experimentation customer had been contacted.
Optimizely says less than 5% of its customers were impacted and that it was not a credentials breach.
The 178-organisation count and the script behaviour come from researchers and news coverage, not Optimizely.

Zscaler ThreatLabz (Nov 18) reports more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script across 12 industries, a wider count than the 178 organisations; it names no actor.
recommendations: Customers using Web Experimentation should review the additional guidance Optimizely sent them and contact Optimizely Support with questions.

sources.name: Optimizely status: Web Experimentation Security Incident

events.summary: Optimizely says an unauthorised party exploited a flaw in its Web Experimentation signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects. It reports the flaw fixed and code removed, and on November 18 said under 5% of customers were affected. Researcher Scott Helme counted 178 organisations; coverage says the code skimmed cards and swapped crypto addresses. Krebs, citing Report URI, says about $7,500 was stolen.
events.title: Optimizely script injection reaches 178 organizations' websites

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Optimizely report. The 178-organisation count and the script's behaviour come from a researcher and news coverage, not Optimizely. Status page re-read 2026-11-19: Nov 18 update says remediation complete and under 5% of customers affected. Zscaler ThreatLabz blog read 2026-11-19: more than 450 domains and 3,000 URLs, no attribution.

About 300 unauthenticated and remotely exploitable; 62 critical.

events.title: Oracle E-Business Suite 12.2 flaws CVE-2026-114924 and CVE-2026-114925 chain to unauthenticated code execution
events.summary: Horizon3 says two flaws in Oracle E-Business Suite 12.2.3 to 12.2.15, an authorization bypass (CVE-2026-114924) and a remote code execution bug (CVE-2026-114925), can be chained so an unauthenticated attacker over HTTP runs OS commands. Oracle scores each 9.8 and fixed them in the November 2026 CSPU. Horizon3 reports no exploitation in the wild and no KEV listing.
events.plain: Two serious flaws in Oracle's business software could let an attacker take over a server over the internet without logging in. Oracle has released fixes.
events.exec: E-Business Suite often holds finance and HR data; an unauthenticated remote takeover is a high-impact risk until patched.
events.action: Apply the November 2026 Oracle CSPU for E-Business Suite; until then, restrict network access to EBS HTTP and REST endpoints.

key_findings: Affects EBS 12.2.3 through 12.2.15; each CVE scored 9.8 by Oracle.
Chained, allows unauthenticated OS command execution as the EBS application-server account.
No exploitation reported; not in CISA KEV as of Nov 18 (per Horizon3).
recommendations: Apply the November 2026 CSPU.
Restrict network access to EBS HTTP and REST endpoints until patched.

validation.note: Horizon3 analysis read in full; CIS MS-ISAC 2026-135 (Nov 17) lists both CVEs under E-Business Suite. Oracle's own advisory returned 403 to the automated reader.

events.action: Inventory every Java runtime, including bundled ones, and install the fixed releases (for example 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1), internet-facing systems first. See Rapid7's advisory for compensating controls where patching is not possible.
events.exec: A serious flaw in widely used Java versions, with a CISA alert urging immediate patching; fixes are available.
events.plain: Security firm Rapid7 and the US cyber agency warned of a serious flaw in recent versions of Java that could let outsiders run their own code. Oracle has released fixes.

key_findings: Memory corruption in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM; specially crafted input could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (CISA).
OpenJDK lists releases 17, 21, 25 and 27 as affected; Oracle fixed versions include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1.

Rapid7 gives Oracle's CVSS v3.1 score as 8.1 (High); neither Rapid7 nor CISA reports exploitation in the wild. SecurityWeek (Nov 19) reports attempts: GreyNoise saw over 150 requests from five IP addresses and no successful intrusions on its sensors; Previdian logged nine attempts from six IPs and says its data cannot confirm compromise.
Researchers at Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against several Java applications; Rapid7 says a reliable exploit needs significant extra work.
recommendations: Apply Oracle's November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update or the OpenJDK fixed releases, internet-facing systems first.
Inventory all JDKs and Java runtimes, including bundled ones; use compensating controls such as Base64 input validation where patching is not possible.

events.summary: Rapid7 and CISA warn of CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell), a memory corruption bug in the x86-64 HotSpot JVM Base64 decoder that could allow remote code execution; Oracle released fixes on November 17. events.action: Verify WinRAR and other tools on your network are the publisher's signed copies; apply application allowlisting and code-signing checks, and alert on memory that is read, write and execute at once and on PNGs with truncated headers.
events.exec: Trusted programs can be rewritten into malware carriers whose fingerprint changes every run, so hash-based blocking is weak.
events.plain: Security firm ReversingLabs describes BubbleLoader, malware that edits ordinary programs like WinRAR so they secretly load other malware, and changes its fingerprint every time it runs.

key_findings: BubbleLoader patches the entry point of a benign program and appends two PNG files; the host then decrypts and reflectively loads a final payload in memory.
Hosts seen include WinRAR, x64dbg, Windows Media Player, a Firefox launcher and virtiofs; the post names no victims or sectors and the final payload varies by sample.
Earliest samples date from February 2026, with two activity clusters in mid-September and early October.

It overwrites padding bytes in the payload with timestamp-derived randomness on each run, so the in-memory hash changes every execution, and hooks RtlPcToFileHeader in ntdll so the payload can handle exceptions.
The second PNG is a fake with a truncated header, which ReversingLabs offers as a static detection signal; the post does not say how the altered programs reach victims.
recommendations: Enforce strict application allowlisting and code-signing verification, especially for common utilities such as WinRAR.
Have EDR alert on read-write-execute memory allocated with VirtualAlloc and on protection changes to the ntdll routine RtlPcToFileHeader.
Add static rules for embedded PNGs with a truncated header.
Rely on behavioural memory analysis and entry-point integrity checks, not only static payload hashes.

events.summary: ReversingLabs analysed BubbleLoader, a loader that rewrites a few instructions at a program's entry point and adds two PNG images to turn legitimate software, including WinRAR and Windows Media Player, into a carrier for other malware. It changes its payload's in-memory hash on every run. Samples date from February 2026, with activity clusters in September and October. Delivery method is not stated.

events.summary: SOCRadar reports that a French-speaking operator it calls BabidiGhost spent nine days in November 2026 targeting European banks, insurers, payment providers and municipalities through a jailbroken AI agent, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland. According to SOCRadar, the agent held 23 archives, about 8.6 GB, belonging to more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies, and an unpatched Metabase instance vulnerable to CVE-2023-38646 let it into one victim. Victims are not named.
events.plain: Security firm SOCRadar says one attacker used a jailbroken AI agent to go after European banks, insurers and town councils, and that it held about 8.6 GB of files from public bodies.
events.exec: SOCRadar documents an AI agent doing intrusion work for one operator; an unpatched Metabase server was one way in.
events.action: SOCRadar advises treating anything reachable without authentication as already indexed, keeping a web application's process from reading a database superuser password, and hunting logs for 5 to 17 November 2026.

evidence.quote: 23 archives, about 8.6 GB, belonging to more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies
a French-speaking operator who spent nine days in November 2026 targeting European banks, insurers, payment providers and municipalities through a jailbroken AI agent

key_findings: A French-speaking operator SOCRadar calls BabidiGhost used a jailbroken AI agent for nine days, typing 1,801 plain-language orders that the agent relayed as 5,779 requests to its model.

More than 50 organizations and datasets were targeted, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland; of 14 analysed in depth, two were breached, three partly breached, four resisted and five saw reconnaissance only.

Entry came through ordinary weaknesses, not zero-days: an internet-facing Metabase instance vulnerable to CVE-2023-38646, a readable container secret, a weak admin password on a shared storage server and an unauthenticated API route.
MFA, IP allowlisting and server-side validation stopped the agent where they were in place.
SOCRadar says the model API key was revoked on 14 November 2026 and deployed implants checked in until 15 November.
recommendations: Treat anything reachable without authentication as already indexed.
Do not let a web application process read a database superuser password.
Inventory internet-facing tools, and rate-limit SMS and email sending.
Hunt in logs for the 5 to 17 November 2026 window and monitor model API and Telegram traffic.

validation.note: Primary source: SOCRadar's own report (the investigating firm), read in part; GBHackers relays it. No victim is named and no victim statement was read.

review.note: Compared title, date, nine days, 23 archives 8.6 GB, Metabase CVE, countries and advice against SOCRadar and GBHackers
